description: We’re a group of UBC students in Computer Science and Biomedical Engineering, based in Vancouver, who love building software to solve interesting problems.
summary:
EVAres is a web app for planning an astronaut’s walk outside on Mars (an EVA), built for the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge. It covers a 33 × 40 km area of Gale Crater, which includes Curiosity’s whole drive. Everything is built from NASA and USGS data: a 1 m elevation map, HiRISE, CTX and THEMIS imagery, CRISM mineral maps, Curiosity’s waypoints and Navcam photos, and REMS and RAD readings.

A crew picks a start point and science stops. EVAres then gives three routes: fastest, least effort and safest. For each route it shows time, slope, surface, energy, oxygen and radiation. A walk-limit ring shows how far the crew can go and still get back within the suit’s limits with a safety reserve, and each route gets a “turn back by” time. Each point of interest says what Curiosity did there, what it couldn’t do, and what a human could. One example is a six-hour walk across the boxwork ridges, where the rover slipped in sand and left questions unanswered.

This matters because a crew on Mars has no GPS and no quick rescue. Planning a walk around science value, terrain and survival margins together is how humans will safely add to what rovers have found.
details: What it does EVAres is a map-based planner for an astronaut walk (EVA) on Mars. It covers a 33 x 40 km area of Gale Crater, including all of Curiosity's drive from Bradbury Landing to the boxwork ridges it studied in 2025-26. A crew picks a start point and science stops, and EVAres answers three questions: - Which way do we walk? It gives three routes (fastest, least effort, safest), with time, distance, slope, surface, energy, oxygen and radiation for each segment, plus an elevation and slope profile. - Can we make it back? A walk-limit ring shows how far the crew can go and still return within the suit's time, energy and oxygen budget, with a 1/6 safety reserve held back. Each route gets a "turn back by" time. - Where is the science? CRISM mineral maps show where clay, hydrated sulfate and bound water were seen from orbit. Each point of interest says what Curiosity did there, what it couldn't do, and what a human crew could. The app has four modes. Explore shows the rover track, waypoints with Navcam photos, and drill sites. Plan builds and compares routes. Go plays the walk as a simulated astronaut. Layers switches between HiRISE, CTX and THEMIS imagery, slope, elevation, surface estimate, mineral maps and walk-cost maps, in 2D or 3D. Example: the boxwork walk Curiosity spent most of a year at the boxwork, a network of ridges and sand-filled hollows likely formed by groundwater. It drilled three shallow holes, slipped in the sand, and left the main questions open. "Try the boxwork walk" loads a six-hour plan where a crew crosses from hollow to ridge, samples the ridge walls and digs under the sand to bedrock, which the rover could not do. Why it matters A crew on Mars has no GPS and no quick rescue. Planning around science value, terrain and survival margins together is how humans will safely add to what rovers have found. How it works - Routing: A* search over a 2 m grid built from the 1 m USGS Gale DEM. Cost combines slope (20 degree limit), estimated surface type, and a Pandolf load-carriage energy model scaled to Mars gravity. Walk limits use a Dijkstra flood out and back. Routing runs in Web Workers on an 8 km planning window that follows the walk. - Walk model numbers come from Apollo, Artemis suit specs, BASALT analog EVA flight rules and NASA JSC studies. They are all listed in the repo and can be changed in config files. - Data checks: at all 1389 Curiosity waypoints, map elevation matches the rover's to a median of 2.7 cm, and our slope matches the rover's tilt to a median of 1.7 degrees. The CRISM scenes are aligned to HiRISE automatically. - Tools: TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL (with 2D and 3D terrain generated in the browser), Zustand, Tailwind, Vite, Hono on Cloudflare Workers, a Node.js data pipeline (sharp) that downloads and prepares all data ahead of time. Honest limits The surface map is an estimate from orbit, not ground-truthed. The oxygen tank size is a placeholder because no Mars suit tank is defined. Boxwork ridges are hand-placed because the DEM barely resolves them. All of these are labelled in the app.
